title: The tenant scope of a tool call arrives as a model-filled parameter, so isolation is decided in the prompt instead of from the authenticated session
problem: My tool takes workspace_id as an argument because that is what the underlying API takes, so the thing choosing which tenant's data to read is the model, and a wrong or coaxed value is a well-formed request my server will happily serve.
symptom: One tenant's records appear in another tenant's agent answer or summary, the server access log shows a syntactically valid authorised call, and there is no failed-authorisation event anywhere because the scope arrived as data rather than being derived from the caller.
why_now: Tool schemas are generated from function signatures, and the fastest way to expose an existing multi-tenant API as a tool is to mirror its parameters, which puts the tenant key in the model-visible argument list. The agent frameworks do provide a non-model channel for exactly this - a local context object that tools receive but the model never sees - yet using it takes deliberate work while the leaky version is the default shape of the code, and the resulting call is indistinguishable from a legitimate one at every layer below the tool.
existing: The OpenAI Agents SDK local context object is passed to tool functions and is documented as never being sent to the LLM, which is the right channel, but nothing prevents a tool from taking the scope as a normal model-visible parameter instead.
MCP authorization requires a server to validate that a token was issued for it, which fixes who the caller is but says nothing about whether the scope inside the tool arguments matches that caller.

Server-side authorisation on the underlying API helps only when the agent's credential is already narrowed to one tenant; a service-wide credential plus a model-supplied scope makes every request legitimate.

evidence.title: Context management - OpenAI Agents SDK
evidence.quote: The context object is not sent to the LLM. It is purely a local object that you can read from, write to and call methods on it.
evidence.note: Fetched 2026-08-18; the page is undated so the date field is the retrieval date. Documents that a non-model channel for tool-visible data exists and is distinct from the LLM-visible argument list. That is what makes a tenant key in a tool signature a choice rather than a necessity, and it is the mitigation this check looks for.

evidence.title: Asana warns MCP AI feature exposed customer data to other orgs
evidence.quote: a software bug in the MCP server exposed data from Asana instances to other MCP users, with the data type being limited to each user's access scope
evidence.note: The consequence class, on a real product: a tenant-isolation defect located in the MCP surface rather than in the product, exposing task data, project metadata, comments and uploaded files across organisations for roughly two weeks. Reported as a logic flaw in the server's own scoping, not an external intrusion. Classed secondary-summary because Asana published no public statement; this is press reporting plus a vendor spokesperson figure, so it evidences that the failure mode occurs in production and does not evidence the specific line of code.

evidence.title: Security Best Practices - Model Context Protocol
evidence.quote: MCP servers MUST NOT accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server.
evidence.note: The spec establishes the principle for identity - a server must not trust an assertion handed to it by its caller - but its normative requirements stop at the token. The scope carried inside tool arguments is left entirely to the implementer, which is the hole this check probes.

build_hypothesis: A tool-registration lint plus a runtime shim: at registration time refuse to publish a tool whose model-visible schema contains a field the framework knows to be a scope key (tenant, org, workspace, account), and require those fields to be bound from the run context instead. The bind is a few lines; the value is that the scope becomes unforgeable by the model and a violation is a startup error rather than a production incident.

check.manual_question: For each tool your agent can call that reads tenant-scoped data, where does the tenant, workspace or account identifier come from - the model's arguments, or a server-side context bound to the authenticated caller? If it is the arguments, what would refuse a call naming a tenant the caller cannot access, and would that refusal show up anywhere?
check.rationale: A tool-decorated function whose parameter list contains a tenant, workspace, organisation or account identifier publishes that identifier in the model-visible schema, which means the model chooses the isolation scope. The mitigation signature is code that binds the scope from a request or run context instead. Known limits: a parameter list containing a nested call with parentheses (a Field or Annotated default) will not match, so this under-reports rather than over-reports; a repo that both binds from context somewhere and takes a scope parameter elsewhere yields MANUAL, which is correct because a partial mitigation is the dangerous case; and a legitimate design where the agent's own credential is already narrowed to one tenant will match this signature, which is why the manual question asks what the credential can reach.
